plain: Zapier and Make are two websites where you build automations by dragging boxes around, with nothing to install on your computer and not a single line of code to write. They work like an intern watching for one thing (an email arriving, someone filling out a form, it turning eight in the morning) and, when it happens, running through the list of tasks you left them. You don't set up or maintain any computer: theirs are on 24/7 and you pay based on how many tasks it does per month. Zapier is the easier of the two and the more expensive one; Make is quite a bit cheaper and looks more like a puzzle of dots connected by lines.

account.free: Both have a genuine free plan and neither asks for a card to start. Zapier free: 100 tasks a month and two-step automations (watch for one thing, do a single thing). Make free: 1,000 operations a month and 2 automations active at once, with as many steps as you want. Once you outgrow it: Zapier runs about $20 a month for 750 tasks and $45-50 for 2,000; Make runs about $9-10 a month for 10,000 operations. Yes, you read that right: for the same money Zapier gives you 750 tasks, Make gives you 10,000. Prices change every few months, so check the pricing page the day you're about to pay.
steps: Orange 'Sign up' button top right. Lets you sign in with Google or any email. No card required.
It asks your job title and 'What apps do you use?'. Answer whatever you want or click 'Skip'. It's only used to show you templates on entry.
Find out about the trial they just gave you

Zapier automatically activates a 14-day trial of the Professional plan. At the top you'll see a notice like 'X days left in trial'. Once it ends you drop to the free plan and everything you've built with more than two steps stops working. It's not a trick, but build knowing it: don't build anything serious during those 14 days.
Open make.com in another tab and sign up the same way

'Get started free' button. Before entering it makes you choose a 'Region': choose a European one if you'll be moving Spanish customer data. That choice can't be changed later from settings; if you get it wrong you'll have to open a new account.
Connect your first app in Zapier

Top left, '+ Create' button and choose 'Zaps'. In the first step search for Gmail or Google Sheets and click 'Sign in'. A Google window opens asking for permissions. Read them: that's exactly where you're granting real access to your email or your spreadsheets.
Find the usage counter before touching anything else

In Zapier: your photo top right, then 'Settings' and 'Usage & Billing'. In Make: left menu, 'Organization', 'Usage' tab. Check it today and check it again in a week. It's the only place that will warn you if this is going to get expensive.
account.warning: Turning on an automation isn't a dry run: it acts on your real data and there's no undo button. If the last step is sending an email, it sends it; if it's deleting a row, it deletes it. The classic accident is the loop: you build something that fires when an email arrives and that in turn sends an email, it bites its own tail, and two hundred messages go out in ten minutes. Zapier detects it and shuts the automation off on its own, but by then you've already burned the month's tasks and your contacts have received the spam. On top of that, connecting your real email account gives it permission to read and write on your behalf until you revoke it by hand. Practice with an email account of your own and a fake spreadsheet, never with the real customer list.

first: Connect a single app, not five. Gmail or Google Sheets, and stop there.
Build the classic two-step flow: when an email arrives with a specific label, add a row to a spreadsheet.
Click 'Test' on each step and really look at the data that shows up on screen: that's where you see what information the app is passing you and under what name.
Turn it on with 'Publish' and send yourself an email to watch it work end to end.
Go back to the usage counter and check how many tasks those three tests cost you. That number is your first lesson in pricing.
words: An automation within Zapier. It's a list of tasks: watch for this, and when it happens, do this other thing.
The same thing as a Zap but in Make. The difference is how it looks: in Zapier it's a top-to-bottom list, in Make it's dots connected by a line you can move around the screen.
What kicks off the automation. Almost never you pressing a button: it's an email arriving, someone filling out a form, or it turning eight in the morning.
Each thing it does after starting: sending the email, logging the row, notifying the chat. These are the ones you pay for.

The unit you're billed on. In Zapier a task is one action that's completed. In Make an operation is each dot the data passes through, and it counts the same even if that dot searches for something and finds nothing.
One full pass of the automation, start to finish, whether it has three steps or forty. It's the unit n8n bills on, which is why its invoice looks so different.

A notice one website fires off to another the moment something happens, instead of asking every fifteen minutes whether it's happened. Make lets you set one up on the free plan; in Zapier, building one yourself by hand requires a paid plan.

The permission you give Zapier or Make to get into your email, your Drive, or your store. Granted once per account and stays alive until you remove it yourself from the connections list. While it's there, the tool can read and write on your behalf even if you have nothing turned on.
matters: You're charged per step executed, not per automation. A six-step flow that fires 400 times a month is 2,000 tasks in Zapier, not 400. The $20 plan includes 750. If you don't do that multiplication on a napkin before building anything, you'll discover it on the bill: people going from $20 to $90 a month without having changed anything, just from selling more.

Nothing is instant on the free plan. Zapier and Make check whether something has happened every fifteen minutes. If you promise a client the chat alert arrives the instant an order comes in, you'll look bad for a solid fifteen minutes straight. What does arrive instantly on any plan is whatever the other app pushes on its own: forms, payments, chat messages.

Turning it on means acting on real data, and the most expensive mistake isn't technical. Nobody breaks something by writing a bad formula; they break it by testing the flow on the real customer list instead of on a fake spreadsheet with three made-up rows.

Where n8n pays off is in the steps, not the volume. n8n charges per full run: a twenty-step flow that runs a thousand times is a thousand executions. In Zapier that same thing is twenty thousand tasks. As long as your flows have two to five steps and fewer than a thousand triggers a month, paying $10-20 is cheaper than your own time setting up and maintaining a server. Once you pass ten steps or several thousand triggers, the difference stops being a matter of opinion and becomes hundreds of euros a month.
ignore: Everything Zapier has hung around the edges: Tables, Interfaces, Chatbots, Canvas. Different products sold from the same dashboard. You don't need them to automate, and they just fill the screen with buttons that don't mean anything to you yet.

The code steps: 'Code by Zapier' and Make's JavaScript modules. They exist and one day will get you out of a jam, but until you've built three or four flows, everything you need is already covered in a normal step.

Branching: 'Paths' in Zapier and the 'Router' in Make, the 'if the customer is premium do this, otherwise do that' thing. A flow with two branches is two flows that can both break at once. First get the straight flow running smoothly.

questions.prompt: You build a six-step flow for your store: an order comes in and, from there, you log the row in a spreadsheet, send the thank-you email, notify the warehouse, generate the invoice, and add the customer to the mailing list. You sell 400 orders a month. You're on Zapier's roughly $20 plan that includes 750 tasks. What's going to happen?

options.text: You'll run out of tasks around day 12: it's five actions per order, 400 orders, 2,000 tasks.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is in the first step. What watches for orders isn't billed in Zapier; only actions that complete are counted. That's why it's five and not six. With 2,000 tasks you need the $45-50 plan or you need to cut steps: for instance, if the invoice is generated from the spreadsheet itself, logging the row and generating the invoice could be a single step.

options.text: You've got plenty of headroom: 400 orders are 400 tasks and you have 350 to spare.
options.why: It's what everyone thinks the first time, and it's not a silly idea: that's exactly how n8n works, where one full run counts as one unit. It breaks because in Zapier the counter moves on every action that finishes, so the same job costs five times what you calculated.

options.text: It's 2,400 tasks, six per order, and you'll be dry by day 10.
options.why: Close. The multiplication method is right, but you included the step that watches for orders, and that one's free. It's 400 tasks a month off: doesn't change the conclusion, but it does change your numbers right when you're choosing between two plans.

questions.explain: Here you don't pay per automation, you pay per step multiplied by how many times it runs. Do that multiplication before building, not after the bill.

questions.prompt: You have a flow that already works: twelve steps, firing 3,000 times a month. Your Zapier bill has climbed into the hundreds of euros and the boss is asking questions. What do you do?

options.text: You move it to n8n, or at least to Make, because n8n charges per full run: 3,000 runs are 3,000, not 36,000 steps.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is the timing. Twelve steps times 3,000 triggers is exactly the profile where Zapier's pricing model crushes you. n8n's paid, hosted version runs around $20-25 a month for several thousand runs, and it doesn't matter whether the flow has twelve steps or forty. If you don't want to switch tools, Make is the middle ground: it still charges per step, but each step costs much less.

options.text: You upgrade your Zapier plan and that's it, between plans there's only about $30 difference.
options.why: It sounds reasonable because between the first few plans the gap really is about $30. It breaks further up: the tens-of-thousands-of-tasks plans stop climbing by $30 at a time. And above all, your bill climbs again every time you add a step to the flow, not just when you sell more. You're renting complexity, not volume.

options.text: You split the flow into three four-step automations so each one uses less.
options.why: Sounds obvious: shorter flows, less consumption. But all three still run for every order, and on top of that you need extra steps to chain one to the next. You end up spending the same or more, with three separate things that can each break on their own and a mess figuring out which one failed.

questions.explain: The price of these tools doesn't depend on how clever your flow is, but on how many pieces it has times how many times it runs. Once that multiplication spikes, the one that charges per full run wins.

shortcuts: Trigger and Action

The two words that structure everything. The trigger is what's being watched ('when an email arrives with this label'); the actions are what happens next ('create a row', 'send a message'). A Zap has one trigger and as many actions as you want. If you find yourself wanting two triggers, that's really two Zaps.
The 'Test' button on each step

Runs that step alone, with real data, and shows you on screen exactly what comes out of it. It's the single most important tool on the whole platform: the field names you see there are what you'll be able to use in the following steps. Never build three steps in a row without testing the first one.
'Zap History' / the run history

The list of every time it's fired, with its status: success, error, filtered, or held waiting. This is where you investigate any 'it didn't work'. Each line can be opened to see the data that went in and out of each step.
'Filter': only continue if...

A step that cuts the flow off when a condition isn't met. It's the piece that prevents 90% of disasters: 'only continue if the amount is greater than 0', 'only continue if the email isn't internal'. Put it as early as possible, right after the trigger, so you're not wasting tasks or touching anything unnecessary.
'Paths' vs 'Filter'

The filter cuts or doesn't cut. Paths branch: if it's type A do this, if it's type B do that. Paths are a paid feature in Zapier. While you're learning, two Zaps with two different filters do the same thing for free and are easier to understand.
'Formatter'

A step that doesn't talk to any app: it transforms data. Putting a date in another format, splitting a full name into first and last, lowercasing, trimming spaces, pulling a number out of text. Before asking an AI to do anything strange, check whether the Formatter already does it: it's instant and free.
'Delay'

Waits before continuing: five minutes, a day, or until a specific time. Its most useful use isn't the obvious one: it gives the other app time to finish creating something, and it stops you sending three notifications in a row when three things arrive together.
'Turn on Zap' (the toggle top right)
A tested but off Zap does nothing, and it doesn't warn you. Constantly forgotten. After turning it on, trigger the real case once yourself and check in the history that it fired on its own.
Tasks and the plan counter

Every action that runs successfully consumes a task. The trigger doesn't count; filters that cut things off don't either. A four-action Zap that fires a hundred times a month is four hundred tasks. It's the number that decides your bill: check it before building loops.
'Duplicate Zap'

Before reworking a Zap that's working, duplicate it and work on the copy. It's your only backup: there's no version history you can roll back to like in Git. Name the copy with the date and what it was for.
daily: Always start from the end. Write in one sentence what you want to exist once it's done ('a new row in the leads sheet and an alert in Slack'). Building boxes without that sentence written down is how you end up with automations nobody knows the purpose of.

One filter right at the start, always. Right behind the trigger, cut off what doesn't belong: internal emails, zero amounts, tests. Without that filter, the first day of real use you'll send messages to real customers for cases that shouldn't have gone through.
Test every step before adding the next. The temptation is to build all six steps and hit test at the end. When it fails, you won't know which of the six it was. Step, Test, look at the data, next.

Really look at the Test data, not just the green checkmark. That's where you discover the 'date' field arrives as text, that the name comes with leading spaces, or that the email arrives nested inside another field. That saves you the errors that show up three weeks later.

Watch out for loops between apps. A Zap that writes to a spreadsheet and another that fires when that spreadsheet changes can call each other nonstop until they burn through the month's plan in one afternoon. Before turning it on, sketch out who triggers whom.
Name your Zaps for whoever reads them a year from now. 'Gmail → Sheets' says nothing. 'Web leads to sales sheet + Slack alert' does. In a list of thirty Zaps, the name is the only thing you'll have.

When something gets repetitive or complicated, look at n8n. Zapier and Make are perfect for connecting four apps without touching anything. When you need loops, real logic, or the volume is driving up the bill, that's the moment to move to n8n, not before.

templates.name: The design sheet you fill in BEFORE touching the platform
templates.what: Half a page of text answering the six questions that determine whether the automation will work or cause problems. Takes five minutes to fill in and saves whole afternoons. Works equally for Zapier, Make, or n8n, and it's also what you paste to an AI when asking for help building it.
templates.how: 1) Copy this into a note. 2) Fill it in plain English, without thinking in boxes or apps. 3) If you can't answer 'how do I know it worked', don't build anything yet: that's the sign the process isn't clear. 4) Once you have it, then open Zapier and build it. 5) Save it alongside the Zap: six months from now it'll be the only explanation of why it's built that way.
fill: Trigger
Exactly what has to happen for this to start. The more specific, the fewer false triggers
Filter
Which cases must NOT go through. Write here what should never make it to execution
Actions
What happens, in order. One line per action, in plain language
Verification
How you'll know tomorrow that it worked. If you can't verify it, you can't maintain it
If it fails
What happens if it breaks halfway: something's lost, duplicated, or left half-done. And who finds out
Volume
How many times a month it will fire. Multiply by the actions and you'll have the tasks it consumes
templates.code:
# ── Automation sheet ──────────────────────────────────────

NAME:  Web leads to spreadsheet + sales rep alert

1. TRIGGER
   When an email arrives at sales@ with the "web" label.

2. FILTER (only continue if...)
   - Sender is NOT from our own domain.
   - Subject does NOT contain "test" or "testing".

3. ACTIONS, in order
   1) Extract name, email, and phone from the email body.
   2) Add a row to the "leads" sheet, log tab.
   3) Notify the #leads-alerts channel with name and email.

4. HOW I KNOW IT WORKED
   There's a new row in the sheet AND a message in the channel,
   with the same email in both places.

5. IF IT FAILS HALFWAY
   The row may end up created without the alert sent.
   Not serious: the lead isn't lost, only the alert.
   I check the history every Monday.

6. VOLUME AND COST
   About 60 leads a month x 3 actions = 180 tasks/month.

7. PERSONAL DATA
   Yes: name, email, and phone of individuals.
   Phone isn't sent to Slack, only to the sheet.

templates.name: The fire test before turning on the Zap
templates.what: A list of seven checks you can run through in ten minutes that catch what breaks on the first day of real use. Ordered from most to least serious: the first three are the ones that cause messages going out to customers who shouldn't have received them.
templates.how: 1) Run through them one by one with the Zap still OFF, using the Test button. 2) For testing, use fake data you'll recognize ('Test Test', test@example.com). 3) After passing them, turn it on and trigger ONE real case yourself, watching the history. 4) Only after that real case comes out fine do you tell others it's working.
fill: The empty case
What happens if the trigger fires with no data, or with half the fields blank
The repeated case
What happens if the same case comes in twice in a row. Does the row get duplicated? Does the alert get sent twice?
The case that shouldn't go through
An internal email, a test, a zero amount. Should get cut off at the filter, not reach the end
Odd text
Accents, special characters, emoji, quotation marks, a 200-character name. This is where spreadsheets and messages break
The outage
What happens if the last step's app is down. Does anyone find out or does it get lost silently?
templates.code:
# ── Before turning on: seven tests ───────────────────────

[ ] 1. CASE THAT SHOULDN'T HAPPEN
      Trigger a case the filter is supposed to cut off.
      Correct = history marks it "filtered", and NOTHING
      shows up in the sheet or the chat.

[ ] 2. DUPLICATE CASE
      Fire off the same case twice.
      Decide beforehand what's correct: two rows or one?
      If it should be one, you need a check before creating.

[ ] 3. REAL BUT EXTREME CASE
      Name with accents and special characters, long text, an emoji.
      Check how it looks in the sheet and in the message.

[ ] 4. INCOMPLETE CASE
      Phone and last name are missing.
      Correct = it's created anyway, with blank gaps,
      without the Zap blowing up.

[ ] 5. THE TEST DATA, ACTUALLY LOOKED AT
      Open each step's result and check that
      each field carries what you think it carries.

[ ] 6. THE TASK COUNT
      Actions x triggers per month. Does it fit your plan?

[ ] 7. THE FAILURE ALERT
      Account settings > error notifications.
      Make sure it reaches an email someone actually reads.

# AND NOW: turn it on, trigger a real case, and watch it.

errors: The Zap is on and never fires

Almost always the trigger isn't what you think it is. Triggers like 'new email' or 'new row' check every X minutes (between 1 and 15 depending on the plan), not instantly: wait before declaring anything dead. And many triggers only see what happens AFTER the Zap is turned on; whatever was already there doesn't get processed. Check the history to see if anything shows up, even marked as filtered: if not even that shows up, the problem is the trigger, not the steps.
It fires but the history marks it 'Filtered'

Your filter is cutting off cases that should go through. Open that run in the history and look at the data that came in: almost always it's an extra space, capitalization ('Web' vs 'web'), or a field arriving empty. Use 'contains' instead of 'exactly matches' when comparing text written by people.
Could not find the field / the field arrives empty at step 3

The previous step doesn't return what you thought. Go back to that step's Test and look at the exact field names it outputs. It's very common for the data to be nested (inside another field) or for the app to call it something else. Never type a field name by hand: always select it from the list the platform offers.
The app returned 'Authentication failed' / need to reconnect the account

The connection to the app expired or the password was changed. Go to 'My Apps', find that connection, and click 'Reconnect'. Important warning: while it was down, cases did NOT wait around; they were lost. Check the history to see since when it's been failing and recover those days' data by hand.
Task limit reached / plan ran out mid-month

You've used up the month's tasks and the Zaps stop. Usually means one of two things: either your volume is higher than you calculated, or you have a loop. Before upgrading your plan, check the history and look for repeated runs of the same case: two Zaps firing off each other can burn a thousand tasks in one afternoon. A well-placed filter at the start saves more money than any plan upgrade.
Duplicate rows or messages get created

The trigger saw the same case twice (an email marked unread, a row edited after being created). Fix it by checking before creating: a search step for a unique piece of data (the email, the order number) and a filter for 'only continue if not found'. In Zapier that's 'Find or Create'. If duplicates matter to you, this isn't optional.
Text arrives with \n, with &, or with HTML tags inside

You're coming from an email or a web form and you're carrying over the source formatting. Add a 'Formatter' → 'Text' → 'Remove HTML tags' step, or whichever applies, before writing it to the sheet or sending it by chat. It's one more step and consumes one task, but it's the difference between readable data and junk.
Works in Test but fails for real

The Test uses a specific case you picked, almost always well-formed. Real life brings empty fields, very long texts, and cases you hadn't imagined. When this happens, open the failed run in the history, compare its data with the Test's, and you'll spot the difference in two minutes. That's why the checklist above includes the incomplete case and the extreme case.

prompts.name: Design the automation before opening the platform
prompts.prompt: Act as the technical person helping me out. I want to automate a process with Zapier or Make and I want to think it through properly before dragging boxes around, because I know building first and thinking later is how you end up with automations that do weird things. I don't know how to code. First ask me whatever questions you need, one at a time, about what the process is, who does it by hand today, how often it happens, and which apps are involved. Then give me the following. One: the exact trigger to use and why that one and not another, warning me if it's one of the kinds that only sees what happens from the moment I turn it on. Two: the filters that need to go right after the trigger so it doesn't run on cases that don't belong, written exactly as I'd type the condition. Three: the list of actions in order, in plain language, one line each. Four: tell me at which points in the flow it could stop halfway and what would happen then: whether something gets lost, duplicated, or nobody finds out. Five: calculate how many tasks a month this will consume with my volume, and tell me if it fits the free plan. Six: tell me honestly whether this specific case is going to outgrow Zapier and I should build it directly in n8n instead, and what signal you're basing that on. My process is: [DESCRIBE IT IN PLAIN LANGUAGE, THE WAY YOU'D TELL A COWORKER].

prompts.name: Figure out why a Zap isn't doing what it should
prompts.prompt: I have an automation built in [ZAPIER / MAKE] that isn't working as expected and I don't know where to start looking. I don't know how to code: walk me through it step by step, asking me one thing at a time, and start with the most likely cause. Before proposing any change, ask me for what you need: which trigger I'm using, what the run history says (whether the run shows up, whether it shows as an error, filtered, or successful), and the exact data that went in and out of the step where it breaks. Once you have it clear, tell me: one, what's happening in plain language; two, whether the problem is in the trigger, a filter, a mislinked field, or the destination app; three, how to fix it, with concrete clicks; four, how I verify it's fine now with a test that doesn't affect real data; five, what test I should have run before turning it on that would have caught this. And also tell me whether, while this has been failing, any information has been lost that needs recovering by hand, because that's what worries me most. What should happen is: [DESCRIBE IT]. What actually happens is: [DESCRIBE IT].

prompts.name: Audit an inherited automation nobody understands
prompts.prompt: I've inherited an automation someone else built and I don't trust it. I'll describe the steps I see on screen. I want an honest audit, no sugarcoating, ranked by severity. Answer me like this. One: explain in plain language what this does start to finish, as if telling someone who's never seen this tool. Two: tell me what cases would make this misbehave: what happens if an empty field arrives, if the same case arrives twice, if one of the apps is down, if someone renames a spreadsheet column. Three: flag anything sending personal data somewhere it shouldn't be, or writing to a production system without any prior check. Four: tell me which steps consume tasks unnecessarily and could be removed or merged. Five: tell me what's missing: filters that should be there, failure alerts that don't exist, duplicate checks. Six: tell me whether this should stay here or whether, given its complexity, it already calls for n8n, and if the answer is 'leave it where it is', say so plainly. The steps I see are: [DESCRIBE THEM ONE BY ONE].

prompts.name: Move from Zapier to n8n without breaking anything
prompts.prompt: I have an automation running in [ZAPIER / MAKE] and I'm considering moving it to n8n, either because the cost has gotten out of hand or because I need to do things I can't do here. I want a reasoned decision, not a sales pitch for switching. First, tell me honestly whether it's worth it in my case: ask me how many runs a month I have, what I'm paying, what exactly I can't do right now, and who's going to maintain this if I go on vacation. If after hearing me you think I should stay where I am, tell me clearly and explain which three tweaks would make it keep working. If you think it is worth it, then give me: one, a step-by-step equivalence table between what I have now and n8n's nodes; two, what things have NO direct equivalent and how they're solved; three, which credentials I'll have to recreate and which ones cause the most trouble; four, the order to do the move in so that at no point do cases go unprocessed, including how long it makes sense to run both systems at once and how I avoid actions getting duplicated during those days; five, how I verify the new version does exactly the same thing as the old one before turning the old one off. My current automation does: [DESCRIBE IT].
